analysis_note: All documents are paraphrased or original summaries; no extended quotation of copyrighted sources.

documents.source_line: Summary of the Tennessee Valley Authority Act's stated purposes (original treatment)
documents.sourcing_note: An original summary of the legislation's public aims; purpose of the act was regional uplift. Its language of progress and planning represents the pro-dam case at its most idealistic.
documents.text_or_description: The TVA was created to tame the floods of the Tennessee River, generate cheap electricity, and lift one of America's poorest regions out of poverty through planned development — a promise that government engineering could remake both nature and society.

documents.source_line: Summary of a U.S. Bureau of Reclamation statement on the Hoover (Boulder) Dam project (original treatment)
documents.sourcing_note: An original summary of the builder's case; purpose is to justify a massive public expenditure during the Depression. Jobs, water, and power are the classic benefits claimed for big dams.
documents.text_or_description: The dam would put thousands of unemployed men to work, store the Colorado River's floods, and deliver water and electricity to farms and cities across the Southwest — turning a desert waste into productive land.

documents.source_line: Paraphrased account of Nubian families displaced by the Aswan High Dam, Egypt
documents.sourcing_note: A paraphrase of displaced people's testimonies collected by journalists and scholars; purpose is to record the human cost. Those who lost ancestral villages experienced the dam as catastrophe, not progress.
documents.text_or_description: We were taken from the villages where our grandfathers are buried and settled in desert lands we did not know. The government promised new houses and fields, but the soil was poor and the water far. The lake swallowed our date palms and our history.

documents.source_line: Jawaharlal Nehru, prime minister of India, on large dams (paraphrased)
documents.sourcing_note: India's leader speaking to his nation; purpose is to inspire faith in modernization. His famous 'temples' language shows how dams became symbols of post-colonial national pride, not just engineering.
documents.text_or_description: Nehru called great dams the temples of modern India, monuments to the nation's resolve to conquer poverty through science and planning. To build them was an act of patriotism; to question them, near disloyalty.

documents.source_line: Findings of the World Commission on Dams (paraphrased)
documents.sourcing_note: An independent international commission reviewing the global record; purpose is assessment, not advocacy. Its numbers gave critics authoritative evidence after decades of anecdote.
documents.text_or_description: The Commission found that large dams had displaced some 40 to 80 million people worldwide, that their electricity and irrigation benefits often fell short of projections, and that the poorest communities bore the costs while distant cities reaped the power.

documents.license: Public domain (U.S. federal government work, Wikimedia Commons)
documents.source_line: Aerial photograph of the Hoover Dam
documents.sourcing_note: A U.S. government photograph; purpose is to document and celebrate the achievement. The dam's sheer scale in a stark desert canyon visualizes both the engineering triumph and the audacity of reshaping a river.
documents.text_or_description: The aerial view shows the great curved concrete wall spanning Black Canyon, holding back the vast blue reservoir of Lake Mead amid bare desert mountains — human engineering imposed on an arid landscape.

documents.license: Public domain (U.S. federal government work; copyright not renewed)
documents.source_line: TVA diagram of its water-control system
documents.sourcing_note: A government planning diagram; purpose is to show mastery — every dam, reservoir, and channel in its place. The tidy schematic embodies the planner's faith that nature can be managed like a machine.
documents.text_or_description: The diagram maps the Tennessee Valley's chain of dams, reservoirs, and navigation channels as one integrated system, each structure labeled and linked — a portrait of a river entirely reorganized by human design.

prompt: Using the documents and your knowledge of world history, evaluate the extent to which large hydroelectric dam projects have benefited or harmed societies in the twentieth century.

analysis.complexity: Multiple paths: weigh benefits (electricity, flood control, jobs, national pride — Docs 1, 2, 4) against harms (displacement, ecological damage, unmet promises — Docs 3, 5); corroborate the pro-dam case across Docs 1, 2, and 4, then contrast with Docs 3 and 5; qualify by asking who benefited vs. who paid (urban consumers vs. displaced villagers); Docs 6 and 7 together show the scale that made both the benefits and harms so large.
analysis.sourcing: Doc 1 (purpose: legislation selling a vision); Doc 2 (audience: a Depression public desperate for jobs); Doc 3 (point of view: the displaced, recorded secondhand); Doc 4 (context: a new nation proving itself); Doc 5 (purpose: an independent audit, decades later).

rubric_map.contextualization: Situate big dams within 20th-century developmentalism: the New Deal's faith in planning, post-colonial nations' drive to industrialize, Cold War competition in foreign aid (U.S. vs. Soviet dam projects), and the rise of environmental movements questioning such projects by the 1970s-1990s.

evidence.describe: All seven describable; strongest: Docs 1, 2, 4 (the promise), Docs 3, 5 (the reckoning), Docs 6, 7 (the scale).
evidence.outside: Outside evidence: the Three Gorges Dam (over a million displaced); the Aral Sea disaster from Soviet irrigation; siltation and the Nile delta's erosion after Aswan; dam failures (Banqiao, 1975); the Narmada Bachao Andolan protest movement in India; rural electrification's effects on quality of life.
evidence.support: 'Benefited' line: Docs 1, 2, 4, 6, 7. 'Harmed' line: Docs 3, 5. Doc 5 (the Commission) is the strongest harm evidence because it aggregates the global record.

rubric_map.thesis: An arguable thesis takes a position on 'extent' with a line of reasoning, e.g., the sample below.

sample_thesis: Large hydroelectric dams benefited societies substantially by delivering electricity, flood control, and jobs on a scale no alternative could match in the twentieth century; however, the benefits came at a severe cost, because the displacement of tens of millions and the ecological damage fell on the poorest communities while the power flowed to distant cities, making the dams' legacy deeply unequal.
title: Hydroelectric Dams in the Twentieth Century
